Neonates of the Rock horned lizard (Phrynosoma ditmarsi) emerge at a remarkably diminutive size, with a snout-vent length at hatching of approximately 2.1 centimeters [Lb = approximately 2.1 centimeters] and a corresponding wet weight at birth of just 0.9 grams [Wwb = 0.9 grams]. These values, recorded from captive-born individuals under controlled thermal conditions, indicate that hatchlings are among the smallest within the genus Phrynosoma, reflecting a life history strategy that prioritises early independence over extended parental provisioning. The neonatal mass is particularly striking given that adult females can attain a maximum wet weight of 36 grams [Wwi = 36 grams], suggesting a nearly forty-fold increase in body mass over the lizard's lifetime. Such a dramatic ontogenetic trajectory implies a prolonged period of rapid somatic growth, during which individuals must secure sufficient arthropod prey to sustain high metabolic demands. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that this initial size may impose constraints on thermoregulatory capacity and predator evasion during the vulnerable first weeks post-hatching, although the specific behavioural adaptations of P. ditmarsi hatchlings remain poorly documented in field settings.

Sexual maturation in Phrynosoma ditmarsi is characterised by pronounced dimorphism in both size and timing between the sexes. Females typically attain reproductive maturity at a snout-vent length of 6.7 centimeters [Lp = 6.7 centimeters] and a corresponding wet weight of 29 grams [Wwp = 29 grams], whereas males achieve puberty at a smaller body size, with a snout-vent length of 5.8 centimeters [Lp = 5.8 centimeters] and a wet weight of 19 grams [Wwp = 19 grams]. This divergence in maturation thresholds is consistent with patterns observed across many iguanian lizards, where female reproductive success is tightly linked to body volume and thus to the capacity to accommodate a clutch of developing eggs. The relatively large size required for female puberty implies that a substantial proportion of the growth trajectory is completed before any reproductive investment begins. From a physiological standpoint, the attainment of these size thresholds coincides with the onset of gonadal activation, triggered by an interplay of somatic growth and seasonal environmental cues, though the proximate mechanisms regulating this transition in P. ditmarsi have not been explicitly investigated.

Under standardised laboratory conditions maintained at a constant 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the Rock horned lizard exhibits a maximum reproductive output of approximately 10 offspring per year [Ri = approximately 10 offspring per year]. This value represents the theoretical upper bound of reproductive effort when thermal conditions are not limiting. In practice, such a sustained rate of offspring production would impose considerable energetic costs on gravid females, particularly given that females must reach a substantial body mass of 29 grams [Wwp = 29 grams] before initiating their first reproductive bout. The physiological capacity to maintain this frequency likely depends on continuous access to high-quality prey items, as well as on the efficient assimilation of nutrients during the active season. It remains unclear whether wild populations of P. ditmarsi can approach this laboratory-determined maximum, given the unpredictable precipitation patterns and fluctuating thermal environments characteristic of its Sonoran habitat.

Long-term captive studies conducted at 25 °C [T = 25 °C] indicate that the maximum lifespan of Phrynosoma ditmarsi extends to approximately 10 years [am = approximately 10 years], a relatively protracted duration for a lizard of its body size. This longevity is consistent with a slow-paced life history strategy, in which delayed maturation and repeated reproductive events are favoured over a single, high-investment breeding season. Under the same thermal regime, the age at which individuals first reproduce is recorded at 2 years after hatching [tR = 2 years after hatching], marking the transition from a purely somatic growth phase to one that encompasses both maintenance and reproductive effort at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. The interval between hatching and first reproduction represents a critical window during which juveniles must nearly achieve their asymptotic body size while simultaneously developing the physiological systems necessary for successful gamete production. The extended lifespan, relative to smaller-bodied congeners, suggests that adult mortality rates in the wild may be comparatively low, perhaps due to the species' cryptic coloration and defensive antipredator behaviours, which include the ability to squirt blood from the ocular sinuses.

Adult body size in Phrynosoma ditmarsi appears to stabilise at a maximum snout-vent length of 7.2 centimeters [Li = 7.2 centimeters], a measurement consistent with the upper register of sizes recorded for the genus. This ultimate length is achieved only after several years of growth, as individuals allocate resources toward structural development before shifting energetic priorities toward reproduction. The pronounced difference between the neonatal and asymptotic body sizes underscores the substantial developmental trajectory that defines the species' life cycle. Field surveys of museum specimen series indicate that the largest individuals are typically females, a pattern that aligns with the selective pressures imposed by fecundity selection: larger females can accommodate more eggs per clutch, thereby enhancing lifetime reproductive output. Comparative analyses with related horned lizards suggest that the relatively modest adult body size of P. ditmarsi may reflect an adaptive response to the specific prey base available in its arid montane habitat, where ant colonies represent the dominant food resource and may impose an upper energetic constraint on attainable size.
